While hindsight reveals the moral failings and racial biases of these policies, their advocates could scarcely predict the nuanced critique of hereditary traits or the civil rights revolutions of later decades. Their credence in eugenics, for better or worse, reflected a deep—and politically potent—desire to optimize society through science.

The historical eugenics programs, though ethically indefensible today, were enacted with the intent of advancing societal well-being as understood by the limited knowledge and societal norms of the early 20th century. They aimed to address urgent social and economic challenges through what was perceived as rigorous science, backed by legal authority and medical consensus. Eugenicists applied this biological concept to complex social behaviors. They argued that traits like intelligence and morality were fixed and hereditary. Consequently, they believed that "defective" individuals would inevitably produce "defective" offspring. Eugenicists argued that the "best" human stock (white, Northern Europeans) was having fewer children, while the "worst" stock (Southern and Eastern Europeans, immigrants, and racial minorities) was reproducing at higher rates. This was often termed "race suicide." Forced sterilization was seen by proponents as a necessary tool to maintain the racial composition and dominance of the United States.
